The authors propose training a separate classifier for each variable in the dataset, using all other variables as predictors. These classifiers are then used to compute Shapley values, which quantify the contribution of each predictor variable to the prediction of the target variable. These Shapley values are then integrated into the BIC score, effectively acting as a soft weight on the complexity penalty. The intuition is that edges with higher Shapley values, indicating a stronger influence, will be penalized less, thus favoring directed edges that align with the data-generating mechanisms. The method is evaluated on ten benchmark discrete Bayesian networks, ranging from 6 to 76 variables, and across seven sample-size regimes. The empirical results demonstrate that XBIC consistently outperforms existing methods, such as BIC-HC, PC, and GES, in terms of oriented-edge F1 score and structural Hamming distance.
